02
WS1 - Cloud account and server stand-up
  • How to do this
    Clicks

    AWS is the company that rents us the server. MFA = a second login code (from a phone app) so the account can't be hijacked by a password alone.

    1. Go to aws.amazon.com → Create an AWS Account, using a company email (not personal).
    2. In the account, turn on MFA for the root login (Security Credentials → assign an authenticator app).
    3. Under IAM/Account, give Tanya billing access.
    Done when: you can sign in with the phone code and Tanya can see billing.
  • How to do this
    Clicks

    The budget alarm emails you if spend ever crosses $25 (it should sit near $15). CloudTrail is a log of who did what in the account - turn it on day one so there's a record.

    1. AWS console search bar → Budgets → Create budget → monthly → $25 → your email.
    2. Search bar → CloudTrail → create a trail with default settings.
    Done when: a $25 budget exists and CloudTrail shows "Logging on."
  • How to do this
    Clicks

    Lightsail is AWS's simple "give me a small server" product. "2GB" is its memory size; Ubuntu 24.04 is the operating system; a static IP is a permanent address so it never changes.

    1. AWS search bar → Lightsail → Create instance.
    2. Platform: Linux/Unix; Blueprint: OS Only → Ubuntu 24.04 LTS; plan: the 2GB bundle.
    3. Name it sta-server → Create. Then Networking tab → attach a static IP.
    4. Write down the static IP and today's date (step 5).
    Done when: the instance shows "Running" and has a static IP.
  • How to do this
    Clicks

    IAM users are individual logins so each person (you, Chris, Tyler) signs in as themselves - better security and a clean audit trail.

    1. AWS search bar → IAM → Users → Create user, one per person.
    2. Give them appropriate access and require MFA.
    Done when: each person has their own login (root is only for emergencies).
  • How to do this
    Clicks

    "Ports" are doors into the server. 22 = remote admin login, 80/443 = web pages. Everything else stays shut so there's less to attack.

    1. Lightsail → your instance → Networking tab.
    2. Under firewall, keep only SSH (22), HTTP (80), HTTPS (443); remove anything else.
    Done when: only 22, 80, and 443 are listed.
03
WS1 - Hardening (locking the server down)
  • How to do this
    Build - do with Claude Code

    SSH is the secure remote door into the server. "Key-only" means you log in with a cryptographic key file instead of a password, which is far harder to break. This is command-line work - don't hand-type it blind.

    Paste to Claude Code: "I have a fresh Lightsail Ubuntu 24.04 server at IP <your IP>. Walk me through connecting over SSH, setting up key-only login for my user, disabling password authentication, and then proving a password login is refused. Give me each command and tell me what to expect after each one." Done when: you can log in with your key, and a password login attempt is rejected.
  • How to do this
    Build - do with Claude Code

    ufw is a second firewall on the server itself (belt and suspenders with the Lightsail one). fail2ban automatically blocks anyone who keeps trying to break in.

    Paste to Claude Code: "On my Ubuntu server, set up ufw to allow only ports 22, 80, and 443 and deny everything else, then install and enable fail2ban with sensible defaults for SSH. Give me the exact commands in order and how to confirm both are active." Done when: ufw status shows only 22/80/443 and fail2ban is running.
  • How to do this
    Build - do with Claude Code

    This makes the server patch its own security holes automatically, so it stays safe without you babysitting it.

    Paste to Claude Code: "Enable unattended automatic security updates on Ubuntu 24.04 and show me how to confirm it's working." Done when: automatic security updates report as enabled.
  • How to do this
    Build - do with Claude Code (added 7/9/26)

    Right now SSH and the n8n login page would face the whole internet with fail2ban as the bouncer. A VPN overlay means only your devices can even see those doors - the public internet only ever sees 80/443. Two options: WireGuard (free forever, a little more setup) or Tailscale Standard ($8/user/mo - its free tier is licensed for non-commercial use only, verified 7/8/26). Pick at build time; WireGuard is the no-cost default.

    Paste to Claude Code: "Set up WireGuard on my Ubuntu 24.04 server and my Windows PC so I can reach SSH and the n8n web UI over the VPN only. Then walk me through closing port 22 in the Lightsail firewall and ufw, and restricting the n8n route in Caddy to VPN clients. Prove SSH from the public internet is refused and works over the VPN." Done when: SSH and n8n are reachable over the VPN, port 22 is closed publicly, and step 14's outside scan shows only 80/443 open.
  • How to do this
    Clicks

    A final sanity check that the doors you closed are actually closed, tested from outside.

    1. Ask Claude Code to run a quick port scan against your IP, or use a free online port-check site for ports 22, 80, 443, and one random other (e.g. 3000).
    2. The three should be open/expected; the random one should be closed.
    Done when: only 22/80/443 respond; everything else is closed.
04
WS1 - The software stack (n8n, Postgres, Caddy, kb-mcp)
  • How to do this
    Build - do with Claude Code

    Docker lets the server run each piece of software in its own tidy "container" so they don't conflict. Compose is the tool that starts them all together from one file.

    Paste to Claude Code: "Install Docker Engine and the Docker Compose plugin on my Ubuntu 24.04 server, add my user to the docker group, and show me how to confirm both versions." Done when: docker --version and docker compose version both print a version.
  • How to do this
    Build - do with Claude Code

    2GB of RAM is n8n's documented minimum - the whole stack fits, but it's tight (n8n idles around 300-500MB, Postgres another 200-500MB). Swap is spill-over memory on disk that absorbs spikes, so one big workflow run can't crash the box. Standard practice on a 2GB server.

    Paste to Claude Code: "Add a 2GB swap file to my Ubuntu 24.04 server, make it persistent across reboots with sensible swappiness, and show me how to check memory headroom once my Docker stack is running." Done when: free -h shows 2GB swap active. Re-check headroom once kb-mcp goes live (SOW empirical question 2) - if it's constantly swapping, resize to the 4GB bundle (a reboot, not a migration).
  • How to do this
    Build - do with Claude Code

    This one file describes all four services and how they connect. It's the master recipe for the whole stack - and saving it to GitHub means the server can be rebuilt from scratch anytime.

    The four pieces: n8n runs the automations, Postgres stores data (incl. the meeting digest), Caddy serves web pages + handles HTTPS, kb-mcp is the Shared Brain.

    Paste to Claude Code: "Write a docker-compose.yml for an STA server with four services: n8n, Postgres 16, Caddy 2, and a kb-mcp container. Use named volumes for data, put secrets in an .env file, and wire Caddy as the reverse proxy for n8n and the report site. Then commit it to my sta-server GitHub repo. Explain each section in plain English." Done when: a docker-compose.yml exists locally and in the sta-server repo.
  • How to do this
    Clicks + Build

    Two halves: in Namecheap you point the two web names at the server (clicks); in Caddy you tell the server to answer for them (Claude Code). Caddy then gets the secure-padlock (HTTPS) certificates automatically.

    1. Namecheap → k12sta.com → Advanced DNS → add three A records: host kb, host reports, and host meetings (the WS2b meeting browser at step 35 needs its own name), all pointing to your server's static IP.
    Then paste to Claude Code: "Configure my Caddyfile so kb.k12sta.com routes to the kb-mcp container and reports.k12sta.com serves the reports folder, both with automatic HTTPS." Done when: visiting https://reports.k12sta.com loads with a valid padlock.
  • How to do this
    Build - do with Claude Code

    n8n is the automation tool you'll log into through a browser. It also safely stores the API keys (like the Granola keys) so they're never sitting in plain text. The encryption key is the master key to every stored credential - copy it into the company password manager the moment it's set (step 21b backs up all secrets together).

    Paste to Claude Code: "Set an admin username/password for n8n via environment variables, set the n8n encryption key, set GENERIC_TIMEZONE and TZ to America/Chicago so schedules fire at Central time, and confirm the credentials store is encrypted. Tell me the URL to log in." Done when: you can log into n8n in a browser with your admin account.
  • How to do this
    Build - do with Claude Code

    This proves the server can recover on its own - if it ever restarts, everything should come back without you touching it.

    Paste to Claude Code: "Bring up the docker compose stack, then reboot the server and confirm all four containers (n8n, Postgres, Caddy, kb-mcp) restart automatically and report healthy. Show me the command to check container status." Done when: after a reboot, all four containers show as running/healthy.
  • How to do this
    Build - do with Claude Code (added 7/9/26)

    Six small settings that prevent the most common small-server failures: runaway Docker logs filling the disk (the classic 2GB-box killer), unscanned images carrying known holes, missing browser security headers, a database door that never needed to exist, a single-factor admin login, and surprise breaking updates.

    Paste to Claude Code: "On my Docker server: (1) set json-file log rotation with a max-size so logs can't fill the disk, plus a weekly disk-space check that warns Slack; (2) install a recent Trivy and add a weekly cron scanning all running images, posting findings to Slack; (3) add security headers in Caddy for the report and meeting sites - HSTS, X-Content-Type-Options nosniff, Referrer-Policy, and CSP frame-ancestors; (4) confirm Postgres publishes no public port and is reachable only on the internal docker network; (5) turn on n8n's built-in MFA for my admin account; (6) pin every image to a specific version tag and set a monthly calendar routine to review and update them deliberately. Explain each as you go." Done when: all six confirm - log caps set, first Trivy scan posted, headers visible in the browser dev tools, no public Postgres port, MFA prompt on n8n login, and pinned tags in docker-compose.yml. Note: OS auto-updates (step 13) do NOT update containers - the monthly pinned-version review is the container path.
05
WS1 - Backups and an outside watchdog
  • How to do this
    Clicks

    A snapshot is a full photo of the server. Daily snapshots mean if anything breaks, you can roll back to yesterday in minutes.

    1. Lightsail → your instance → Snapshots tab → enable automatic snapshots.
    2. Set retention to keep the most recent 7.
    Done when: automatic snapshots are on with a 7-day retention.
  • How to do this
    Build - do with Claude Code

    Your automations live inside n8n; this backs them up to GitHub so they're never trapped on the box and can be restored or reviewed.

    Paste to Claude Code: "Set up n8n to automatically export all workflows to my sta-server GitHub repo on a schedule (or via its Git integration). Explain how to confirm a workflow change shows up in GitHub." Done when: a saved n8n workflow appears in the GitHub repo.
  • How to do this
    Clicks

    GitHub holds the compose file but deliberately never the secrets (the .env file stays out of the repo). Snapshots cover normal restores - but a rebuild-from-GitHub without the .env and the n8n encryption key loses every stored credential, including the Granola keys and all staff Shared Brain keys. One secure note closes that hole.

    1. Copy the full contents of the server's .env file (includes the n8n encryption key) into the company password manager as a secure note named sta-server .env.
    2. Update the note any time a secret is added or rotated - make it part of the key-rotation habit (step 47).
    Done when: the secure note exists and matches the server's current .env.
  • How to do this
    Clicks + Build

    The server can't tell you when it's dead - so an outside service pings it and shouts in Slack if it goes quiet. healthchecks.io is free.

    1. Sign up at healthchecks.io, create two checks (one for n8n, one for kb-mcp), and connect its Slack integration.
    2. Your local PC's Cowork scheduled tasks need the same dead-man's-switch - that's Section 11 at the end of this checklist (separate from the server).
    3. Free-tier cap (verified 7/8/26): 20 checks total. These 2 plus the 14-18 local checks in Section 11 land right at the cap - if you run out, consolidate the lowest-value local checks or take the paid tier. Don't split across free accounts (against their terms).
    Then paste to Claude Code: "Wire my server so n8n and kb-mcp each ping their healthchecks.io URL on a schedule, so a missed ping triggers a Slack alert." Done when: both checks show green and a deliberate stop fires a Slack alert.
  • How to do this
    Clicks

    A backup you've never restored isn't a backup. Prove it works once, and make sure someone other than you can do it.

    1. In Lightsail, create a new instance from a snapshot and confirm it boots (then delete the test copy).
    2. Put a monthly restore test and a quarterly "Chris or Tyler restores without Adam" drill on the calendar.
    Done when: a snapshot has been restored successfully at least once.

WS2b - The Granola customer-meeting digest
  • How to do this
    Clicks (in n8n)

    Put the keys you collected in step 4 into n8n's secure credential store so the workflow can use them without exposing them.

    1. In n8n → Credentials → add a Header Auth (or HTTP) credential for each person's grn_ key.
    2. Name them clearly: Granola - Adam, Granola - Chris, Granola - Tyler.
    Done when: three Granola credentials exist in n8n.
  • How to do this
    Clicks (decisions)

    Two simple rules the workflow follows: which meetings count as "customer," and what to do when several of you were in the same meeting.

    1. Customer rule: keep a meeting if any attendee's email is NOT @k12sta.com.
    2. Dedup rule: if several staff attended, keep the organizer's note (fallback: whichever synced first).
    Done when: both rules are written down for the build step.
  • How to do this
    Build - in n8n, with Claude Code

    Picks the time the digest runs each night - after the workday so all meeting notes have finished syncing in Granola first.

    Paste to Claude Code: "In n8n, add a Schedule Trigger that runs once nightly at 9pm Central. This starts the Granola digest workflow. Confirm GENERIC_TIMEZONE is America/Chicago (set in step 18) so 9pm actually means Central." Done when: the workflow shows a nightly schedule trigger.
  • How to do this
    Build - in n8n, with Claude Code

    For each key, the workflow asks Granola for the day's meetings, then drops the internal-only ones.

    Paste to Claude Code: "In n8n, for each of my three Granola credentials, add an HTTP Request to GET https://public-api.granola.ai/v1/notes?created_after=<last run>, then filter to keep only meetings where at least one attendee email is not @k12sta.com. Build this with me node by node." Done when: a test run returns only customer meetings.
  • How to do this
    Build - in n8n, with Claude Code

    Stops the same meeting showing up two or three times when more than one of you recorded it.

    Paste to Claude Code: "Add an n8n step that groups the meetings by calendar event ID and keeps just one per event - prefer the organizer's note, otherwise the first one. Output one record per meeting." Done when: a meeting two of you attended produces a single record.
  • How to do this
    Build - with Claude Code

    Postgres is the database already on your server. This is where the meetings are stored. "Upsert" = update if it already exists, add if it doesn't - so re-runs never duplicate.

    Paste to Claude Code: "Create a Postgres table customer_meetings (meeting title, date, customer/company, attendees, source owner, summary, action items, granola note id, calendar event id) and add an n8n Postgres step that upserts each meeting keyed on calendar event id." Done when: a test run writes rows, and a second run updates instead of duplicating.
  • How to do this
    Build - with Claude Code

    This is the page your team opens to browse every customer meeting. It reads from the Postgres table and sits behind the same staff login as the reports. This is the one piece that's a small web app, not just a config tweak.

    Paste to Claude Code: "Build a simple internal web page served by Caddy at e.g. meetings.k12sta.com that reads the customer_meetings Postgres table and shows a sortable, filterable list (by date, customer, owner) with each meeting's summary, action items, and attendees. Put it behind the same staff token as reports.k12sta.com. Render every meeting field as plain text - never as HTML - since summaries originate in external meetings (XSS)." Done when: the page lists your customer meetings and you can sort/filter them.
  • How to do this

    3. An all-@k12sta.com meeting = no row.

Local system hardening (audit 2026-06-24 follow-up)

Your local PC's Claude system - separate from the server above. From the 2026-06-24 audit. Do these after the server's own watchdog + restore (steps 22-23).

  • How to do this
    Clicks + Build

    Distinct from step 22 (which watches the server's n8n + kb-mcp). These are the tasks under Scheduled\ on your PC - if one silently stops firing, nothing tells you today. A dead-man's-switch on healthchecks.io alerts you when a task misses its check-in.

    1. At healthchecks.io, create one check per active task (14 active per watchdog-setup.md; the SOW's July update counts ~18 recurring jobs - re-count against the live Scheduled\ folder first and update the table). Set each check's Period + Grace to that task's real schedule. Start with weekly-github-backup - the most important.
    2. Copy each ping URL into the table in watchdog-setup.md, replacing PLACEHOLDER_URL.
    3. Mind the free-tier cap: 20 checks total including the server's 2 (step 22).
    Then paste to Claude Code: "Wire these healthchecks.io ping URLs into the scheduled tasks per watchdog-setup.md - add the success-ping block at the end of each task's SKILL.md (weekly-github-backup is the wired worked example)." Done when: each active task pings on success and a deliberately-skipped run raises an alert.
  • How to do this
    Clicks + Build

    Your whole Claude system lives on one PC and backs up to GitHub weekly. You have never test-restored it. An untested backup is a hope, not a backup - and a stale-.git scare already happened this cycle.

    1. Make a scratch folder outside the Claude tree, e.g. Desktop\restore-test.
    2. Clone: git clone https://github.com/abaker421/school-tech-ai-system.git restore-test
    3. Open a couple of key files (the-architect/instructions.md, a KB module) - confirm they are complete and current.
    4. Confirm Knowledge Base/adam/ is NOT in the clone (personal scope stays private).
    5. Delete the scratch folder when satisfied.
    Done when: a clone from GitHub opened clean, key files were current, and adam/ was absent.
